title: Pressure
lead: Pressure is the force divided by the area perpendicular to the force over which it is applied, and a given force can have a very different effect depending on the area it is spread over. This section defines pressure, names the pascal and the other units still in common use, turns a pressure back into a force in a worked example, and explains why the force a static fluid exerts is always perpendicular to the surface it acts on and is exerted on every surface at once.
objectives: Explain the relationship between pressure and force.
Calculate force given pressure and area.
summary_html:
• Pressure is the force per unit perpendicular area over which the force is applied. In equation form, pressure is defined as $\kPr = \frac{\kF}{A}.$
  • The SI unit of pressure is pascal and $1\ \text{Pa} = 1\ \text{N/m}^2$.

exercises.prompt: How is pressure related to the sharpness of a knife and its ability to cut?

answer.solution: Pressure is the force divided by the area the force is applied over, $\kPr = \kF/A$. A sharp knife has an edge whose area of contact with the material is very small, so the same push of the hand makes a very large pressure along the edge, large enough to separate the material there. A dull knife has a wider, rounded edge; the same force is spread over a larger area, the pressure is smaller, and the knife crushes or tears the material rather than cutting it. Sharpening a knife does not change the force you can apply, only the area that force is concentrated on.

exercises.prompt: Why does a dull hypodermic needle hurt more than a sharp one?

answer.solution: The skin gives way at about the same pressure whichever needle is used, so what differs is the force needed to reach that pressure. A sharp needle has a point of very small area, and by $\kF = \kPr A$ the pressure that breaks the skin is reached with a small force. A dull needle has a larger area at its tip, and reaching the same pressure takes a larger force. That larger force is pushed against the skin and the tissue under it, stretching and compressing more of it before the skin gives way, and it is this larger force and the deformation it causes that hurt.

exercises.prompt: The outward force on one end of an air tank was calculated in Example 11.2. How is this force balanced? (The tank does not accelerate, so the force must be balanced.)

answer.solution: The air inside the tank exerts its pressure on every surface it touches, not on one end only, and the force on each surface is perpendicular to it. On the other flat end of the cylinder the same pressure acts on the same area, so the air pushes on it with an equal force, $\kF = \kPr A = 1.22\times 10^{5}\ \text{N}$, in the opposite direction, and the two end forces balance each other. The forces on the curved wall point outward all around the cylinder and cancel in the same way, each one matched by the force on the opposite side. The tank as a whole feels no net force from the air inside it, which is why it does not accelerate; what the air does is stretch the walls of the tank, and that is why the tank must be strong.

exercises.prompt: Why is force exerted by static fluids always perpendicular to a surface?

answer.solution: A static fluid is one that is not flowing, and a fluid by definition yields to a shearing force: it cannot resist a force applied along a surface, and it cannot exert one either. If the fluid pushed on a surface with a force that had a component along the surface, the surface would push back on the fluid with an equal and opposite force along it, by Newton’s third law, and that sideways force would set the fluid flowing. Since the fluid is static and does not flow, no such sideways component can exist, and the only force a static fluid can exert on a surface is the one perpendicular to it.

exercises.prompt: How do jogging on soft ground and wearing padded shoes reduce the pressures to which the feet and legs are subjected?

answer.solution: Each step must supply the force that stops the body’s downward motion and pushes it up again, so the force on the foot is set by the runner’s weight and the way she runs, not by what she runs on. What soft ground and padding change is the area over which that force is spread: the surface deforms under the foot and makes contact with more of it, so by $\kPr = \kF/A$ the same force makes a smaller pressure on the foot and on the joints above it. Padding and soft ground also spread the force out over a longer time as they compress, which lowers the peak force itself, as the chapter on momentum explains.

exercises.prompt: Toe dancing (as in ballet) is much harder on toes than normal dancing or walking. Explain in terms of pressure.

answer.solution: In normal walking the body’s weight is spread over the sole of the foot, or over the heel and the ball of the foot, an area of many square centimeters. On the point of the toes the same weight is supported on the tips of a few toes, an area many times smaller, so by $\kPr = \kF/A$ the pressure on the toes is many times greater. The bones, joints and tissue of the toes have to carry that pressure, which is why toe dancing is so demanding and why a dancer’s pointe shoes are built to spread the load over the toes.

exercises.prompt: How do you convert pressure units like millimeters of mercury, centimeters of water, and inches of mercury into units like newtons per meter squared without resorting to a table of pressure conversion factors?

answer.solution: Each of these units names the height of a column of liquid that the pressure can support, so the conversion is the definition of pressure applied to that column. A column of liquid of height $h$ standing on a base of area $A$ has a volume $Ah$, a mass $\rho Ah$ by the definition of density, and a weight $\rho Ahg$. The pressure it exerts on its base is that weight divided by the area, $\kPr = \rho Ahg/A = \rho gh$, and the area cancels. So a pressure of 1 mm Hg is the pressure of a column of mercury 1 mm high: take the density of mercury from Table 11.1, $13.6\times 10^{3}\ \text{kg/m}^3$, multiply by $g = 9.80\ \text{m/s}^2$ and by the height $1.00\times 10^{-3}\ \text{m}$, and the result, about $133\ \text{N/m}^2$, is the conversion factor. A centimeter of water uses the density of water, $1.00\times 10^{3}\ \text{kg/m}^3$, with a height of $1.00\times 10^{-2}\ \text{m}$, and an inch of mercury uses the density of mercury with a height of $2.54\times 10^{-2}\ \text{m}$. Only the densities and $g$ are needed.

exercises.prompt: As a woman walks, her entire weight is momentarily placed on one heel of her high-heeled shoes. Calculate the pressure exerted on the floor by the heel if it has an area of $1.50\ \text{cm}^2$ and the woman’s mass is 55.0 kg. Express the pressure in Pa. (In the early days of commercial flight, women were not allowed to wear high-heeled shoes because aircraft floors were too thin to withstand such large pressures.)

answer.hint: Her whole weight rests on the one heel, so the force is $m g = (55.0\ \text{kg})(9.80\ \text{m/s}^2)$, and the area must be in square meters: $1.50\ \text{cm}^2$ is $1.50\times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}^2$.

exercises.prompt: Nail tips exert tremendous pressures when they are hit by hammers because they exert a large force over a small area. What force must be exerted on a nail with a circular tip of 1.00 mm diameter to create a pressure of $3.00\times 10^{9}\ \text{N/m}^2?$ (This high pressure is possible because the hammer striking the nail is brought to rest in such a short distance.)

answer.hint: The tip is a circle 1.00 mm in diameter, so its radius is $0.500\ \text{mm} = 5.00\times 10^{-4}\ \text{m}$ and its area is $\pi r^2$; then $\kF = \kPr A$.
